title: Missing Memories
html:
People, Places and a Life in Letters

Pradeep Biswal

Edited, with an Introduction and Notes, by
Ahimanikya Satapathy

title: The Sweetness We Keep
html:
A radio gathers neighbours into a house. A bicycle carries a boy towards the world beyond his village. A book, kept for years, waits for another pair of hands. In Pradeep Biswal’s recollections, life returns through things small enough to hold and generous enough to open a whole landscape. We enter through the familiar and find, slowly, how much it contains.

Gangadhar Meher begins Madhumaya with an invitation:

ବିଶ୍ୱ ଦେଖ ମଧୁମୟରେ ଜୀବନ !
O life, behold the world, filled with sweetness!
— Gangadhar Meher

That invitation offers a way into these pages. Sweetness lives in the company we keep, in a voice remembered, in the discovery that an ordinary day has given us something worth carrying. Biswal’s village holds such abundance, together with the hardship that makes it fragile. Family affection and financial strain share the same rooms. The boy who discovers the pleasures of movement also learns how much effort a life can require.

To receive life as it comes is a patient art. There are days to delight in and days to endure, people to thank and losses for which no explanation is enough. The warmth of these recollections comes from their willingness to keep the whole experience in view. The past is allowed its laughter, its disappointments, its unfinished conversations. Even where hurt remains, the writing continues to make room for other people.

William Blake gives passing joy its own brief radiance in Eternity:

But he who kisses the joy as it flies
Lives in eternity's sunrise.
— William Blake

Memory cannot hold a day still. It can bring us close to what made that day alive. Biswal returns to a radio broadcast, a newspaper, an encounter with a writer, an act of encouragement at work. The pleasure lies in noticing again. A reader may recognise, beneath the particulars of his life, a voice from their own childhood or a kindness whose importance only became clear years later.

The man who emerges is attentive to both companionship and conviction. Public service brings him into the company of mentors, colleagues and people seeking help. Some encounters leave gratitude; others leave a wound. He speaks of both. A pensioner’s appreciation can weigh more in memory than a formal assessment, because it reveals where an institution has touched a life. Such moments connect the officer’s work with the poet’s habit of looking closely.

His own verse gives renewal a modest, living shape. In The Art of Living, after an image of fire across the hilltops, he writes:

Still green leaves
Sprout again
On the branches
— Pradeep Biswal

The word “Still” carries the force of that return. Damage has occurred, and life is beginning again. It is a fitting companion to a memoir in which affection survives disappointment and curiosity continues beyond the demands of a career. Enjoyment here can be an act of persistence: the willingness to listen, to read, to meet another person without letting yesterday’s injury decide everything about tomorrow.

Odia is one of the deepest homes of this life. His attention to its writers, his practice of writing across Odia and English, and his concern for the fate of books reveal an affection sustained through work. To care for a language is to keep entering its conversations: to read those who came before, to listen to those writing now, to help a work find the next reader. In these pages, Odisha has the intimacy of speech, remembered places and people whose words continue to accompany him.

That affection also gives him reasons to speak up. A life welcomed with gratitude still asks us to recognise unfairness, to question a failure of responsibility, to say when someone has been overlooked. His recollections of hurt sit beside his admiration for generosity. We are invited to consider a person making sense of experience, with loyalties, vulnerabilities and judgements that remain open to conversation.

The book follows these connections from childhood into working life, then into the company of writers and the landscapes of their imagination. A personal meeting opens towards a poem; a poem leads back to a river, a town, a question about belonging. Towards the end, concern for inherited books brings us to Dasia Aja, the lover of literature who built a rural library. After so many encounters with writers, we meet someone whose devotion made room for readers.

There is a quiet generosity in that ending. What we have loved can be placed within another person’s reach. Missing Memories asks us to enjoy the life we have been given, attend to the people who share it, and leave something of value behind. A remembered voice, a kindness, a book passed on: these are small ways of keeping a world alive.

title: Where Life Began
html: The village gives these recollections their first scale: a household, a school, a road, the distance a bicycle can carry a child. Family ideals meet the demands of earning, learning and finding a way forward. The opening essays stay close to those early experiences, allowing affection and difficulty to occupy the same remembered ground.

title: A World of Voices
html: Radio and newspapers enlarge the world of the village. Voices arrive from elsewhere, a poem finds listeners, and the young listener eventually enters the studio himself. These overlapping recollections follow the beginnings of a public voice and the people who made broadcasting and print part of everyday life.

title: Learning to Serve
html: Public service first takes shape here through people: an example within the family, an encounter with a political leader, the habits of colleagues and seniors. The work becomes visible in decisions and exchanges. These portraits ask the reader to notice how authority is exercised, how practical knowledge is shared, and how much an institution’s character owes to those who inhabit it.

title: The Work and the Person
html: An assignment can teach more than its official brief. The following recollections move through finance, mentorship, difficult moments and journeys undertaken for public work. Their connections are personal as well as professional. Different accounts return to shared years, gradually bringing into view the relationship between the work an officer performs and the person who carries it.

title: The Measure of a Life
html: Disappointment leaves its own record. These essays give space to the injuries of working life, then turn towards civility, generosity and the recognition that comes from people served. Their movement holds bitterness beside gratitude. By the section’s close, the measure of a career has widened to include those whose thanks may never enter an official file.

title: In the Company of Writers
html: Literary life grows through reading and through encounters: a conversation, an invitation, the encouragement of someone whose work one admires. Here personal portraits sometimes lead directly into critical essays. The shift asks us to linger with a writer’s work after meeting the person, making room for both affection and interpretation.

title: The Landscapes Within
html: A river, a remembered town, a figure from myth: literature gives each a life beyond its immediate setting. These essays move between encounters with writers and readings of the worlds they create. Place gathers feeling; memory enters form. As the focus changes from one writer to another, the reader is invited to listen for the distinct concerns and possibilities of each work.

title: Keeping the Lamp Alight
html: The final essays turn towards the reader and the future of books. Questions about publishing, literary attention and inherited collections lead to Dasia Aja’s library. His place here is as a gatherer and guardian of literature. After so many encounters with those who write, the book closes with the labour that keeps writing available to others.
